anchor.title: [Assembly line at the Ford Motor Company's Highland Park plant]
anchor.creator: Unknown
anchor.citation: [Assembly line at the Ford Motor Company's Highland Park plant], ca. 1913. Photograph. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, SSF - Assembly Line Methods [item] [P&P], LC-USZ62-19261 (b&w film copy neg.). https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2011661021/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: A bustling factory interior with multiple unfinished Ford Model T car chassis on wheels progressing along an elevated moving track. Workers in period clothing stand on the floor and platforms, installing parts like wheels, engines, and body components using tools and hoists amid machinery and conveyor systems in a large industrial hall.
anchor.caption: This photograph captures Ford's innovative moving assembly line at the Highland Park plant in 1913, where unfinished Model T cars roll past workers, revolutionizing mass production and making automobiles affordable for average Americans, a key development in U.S. industrial history.

anchor.title: The Homestead strike, 1892
anchor.creator: Underwood & Underwood
anchor.citation: Underwood & Underwood, _The Homestead strike, 1892_, 1892. 8 photographic prints on stereo cards: stereograph. LOT 7105 (S) [P&P]. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2005684354/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: A paired stereograph image reveals the chaotic aftermath of conflict at Carnegie Steel's Homestead mills: smoke rises from damaged structures near the river, crowds of strikers with rifles line the shore and rooftops watching intently, while uniformed state militia march in formation down a street amid tents and onlookers, capturing the tense military intervention during the 1892 strike. (62 words)
anchor.caption: This 1892 stereograph collection documents the Homestead Steel Strike at Andrew Carnegie's mills, showing the Pinkerton battlefield, strikers guarding against scabs, and arriving state militia, highlighting violent labor conflict during industrialization. (US.11)

anchor.title: John Howell, an Indianapolis newsboy, makes $.75 some days. Begins at 6 a.m., Sundays. (Lives at 215 W. Michigan St.) Location: Indianapolis, Indiana.
anchor.creator: Lewis Wickes Hine
anchor.citation: Hine, Lewis Wickes. \"John Howell, an Indianapolis newsboy, makes $.75 some days. Begins at 6 a.m., Sundays. (Lives at 215 W. Michigan St.) Location: Indianapolis, Indiana.\" Photograph, August 1908. LOT 7480, v. 1, no. 0118 [P&P]. National Child Labor Committee collection. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2018673753/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: A young boy in a flat cap and light shirt stands holding newspapers on a busy urban street corner lined with storefronts and horse-drawn wagons. Streetcar tracks run through the cobblestone road amid pedestrians. Prominently, the photographer's shadow and large camera tripod loom in the foreground across the pavement. (48 words)
anchor.caption: This 1908 photograph by Lewis Hine captures young newsboy John Howell on an Indianapolis street corner, starting work at 6 a.m., highlighting the grueling child labor conditions that fueled Progressive Era reforms in Tennessee US.13 standards.
